analysis.title: USA: FOMC Minutes Note "Almost All" Participants Judged That "Further Action" to Raise the Fed Funds Rate "Would Likely Be Appropriate"
key_insights: October FOMC minutes: "most" participants supported holding the fed funds rate at 3.75-4.00%. "Many" cited the benefits of accumulating additional information before deciding the policy stance. "A few" of these called the hold "a close call."

"Some" participants, including dissenters Governor Cook and President Hammack, favored a 25bp hike. They judged the policy stance "not sufficiently restrictive." "A few" of them warned that delay risked entrenched high inflation or "larger and more disruptive" tightening later.
"Almost all" participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks, further action to raise the target range "would likely be appropriate." This makes a hike the committee's baseline direction.

"A couple" of participants said a hike larger than 25bp could warrant consideration at the next meeting if incoming inflation data were unfavorable. "A few" cautioned that inflation could prove more persistent than anticipated and require a more restrictive stance.

Participants judged inflation to remain elevated. "Most" described pressures as "broad based." The "vast majority" said high energy prices continued to contribute. "Many" said AI-buildout demand was straining supply and raising prices of technology-related consumer goods. "Several" said tariff effects appeared to be waning.
"Several" participants noted that annual revisions to the national accounts lowered measured inflation this year. "A couple" stressed this did not reflect an improved underlying inflation outlook.

Participants generally described the labor market as stable and close to maximum employment. "Many" pointed to signs of modest tightening, "some" noted low labor market dynamism, and "most" judged nominal wage growth "moderate" and broadly consistent with 2% inflation.

Staff forecast: near-term growth strengthened modestly versus September and the medium-term outlook was little changed, with real GDP expected to "slightly outpace potential" through 2028. Inflation is now seen reaching "about 2 percent" in 2028, versus 2029 in the September minutes.

Staff continued to see inflation risks as skewed to the upside. They flagged the possibility that longer-run inflation expectations could have become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation. Risks to growth and employment were seen as "more balanced."

Goldman expects two more 25bp hikes, in December 2026 and March 2027, for three in total and a peak of 4.25-4.50%. A third hike could come earlier in January, or the FOMC could deliver more than three hikes if the next two inflation reports do not show the expected improvement.
